questions.q: In a Max-Cut QUBO, how is the diagonal entry Q_ii for node i determined from the graph?
options: Q_ii equals -1 times the degree of node i (the number of edges touching it)
Q_ii is always equal to 0
Q_ii equals the total number of nodes in the graph
Q_ii equals +2 times the number of edges touching node i
questions.explain: Each edge touching node i contributes -1 to Q_ii (from the -x_i term in -(x_i+x_j-2x_ix_j)), so Q_ii equals -1 times node i's degree -- for example, node 1 in the lab's graph touches 3 edges, giving Q_11 = -3.

questions.q: On the lab's 5-node graph with edges (0,1),(0,2),(1,2),(1,3),(2,4),(3,4), what is the true maximum cut found by brute-force checking all 32 assignments?
options: 6 out of 6 edges
5 out of 6 edges
4 out of 6 edges
3 out of 6 edges
questions.explain: Brute-force confirmation over all 32 possible assignments shows the maximum cut is 5 out of 6 edges -- one edge can never be cut because nodes 0, 1, and 2 form a triangle.

questions.q: Why can a triangle subgraph (3 mutually connected nodes) never have all 3 of its edges cut simultaneously?
options: Because splitting 3 nodes into only 2 groups always forces at least two of the three nodes into the same group, leaving the edge between them uncut
Because triangles are not allowed in Max-Cut problems
Because a triangle has more than 3 edges
Because Q_ii is undefined for nodes inside a triangle
questions.explain: With only 2 groups available for 3 nodes, by the pigeonhole principle at least two of the three nodes must share a group, so the edge connecting that pair is never cut -- which is exactly why this graph's optimum is 5, not 6.

questions.q: For x = (1,1,0,0,1) on the lab's graph, what is f(x) computed from the Q matrix, and how many edges does this assignment actually cut?
options: f(x) = -5, cutting 5 edges
f(x) = -4, cutting 4 edges
f(x) = -6, cutting 6 edges
f(x) = 0, cutting 0 edges
questions.explain: Matrix evaluation gives f(x) = -5, and recounting every edge against x=(1,1,0,0,1) confirms 5 of the 6 edges are cut -- (0,1) is the only uncut edge since nodes 0 and 1 are both in group 1.

questions.q: Why does the mirror assignment x = (0,0,1,1,0) achieve the exact same cut value as x = (1,1,0,0,1)?
options: Because swapping every x_i to 1-x_i only relabels which group is called '0' and which is called '1' -- it never changes which edges end up with endpoints in different groups
Because the two assignments happen to be unrelated but coincidentally equal
Because mirror assignments always reduce the cut value to zero
Because the graph has no edges connecting nodes 3 and 4
questions.explain: Flipping every bit simultaneously swaps the two group labels but preserves which pairs of nodes end up on opposite sides -- so the cut value, and therefore f(x), is unchanged.
